## Deal with the electrical risk first

Water near sockets is dangerous, so do these steps before anything else:

1. Don't touch the sockets, plugs, or the dishwasher if you're standing in water or your hands are wet.
2. Turn off the power at the fuse box/consumer unit. Switch off the circuit for the kitchen, or the main switch if you're unsure which one it is. Only do this if you can reach the fuse box without standing in water.
3. Once the power is off, unplug the dishwasher and turn off its water supply. The valve is usually under the sink or behind the dishwasher.
4. Mop up the water with towels.
5. Don't turn the power back on until the area is completely dry. If water got into the sockets, or you see scorch marks, smell burning, or the circuit keeps tripping, get an electrician to check them first.

If you can't safely reach the fuse box, or water is near the consumer unit itself, keep away and call an electrician or your energy supplier's emergency line.

## Common causes of dishwasher leaks

Once it's safe, these are the usual culprits:

• Door seal (gasket): Cracked, worn, or dirty seals leak from the front. Check the rubber strip around the door.
• Blocked filter: Water backs up and overflows. The filter is usually at the bottom of the tub and twists out for cleaning.
• Wrong detergent: Washing-up liquid or too much detergent causes excess suds that spill out the door.
• Loose or damaged hoses: Check the inlet and drain hoses behind the machine for cracks or loose connections.
• Machine not level: If it tilts forward, water can escape from the door.
• Faulty inlet valve or pump: This is less obvious and often needs a repair technician.
• Blocked sink drain: If the dishwasher drains into the sink plumbing, a blockage can push water back.

## Tips for figuring out where it's coming from

• Front, near the door: Likely the seal, suds, or levelling.
• Underneath or behind: Likely a hose, pump, or valve.
• Only during certain parts of the cycle: Filling points to the inlet, draining points to the drain hose or pump.

If you can't find an obvious cause, or the leak is from inside the machine, call a repair technician. Under the circumstances, it's worth getting those sockets checked too.

its coming from the bottom of the door at the front, loads of suds too. its still running and the water is spreading toward an extension lead on the floor, im scared

## Do this right now

1. Don't touch the extension lead, the dishwasher, or the water. Keep out of the wet area.
2. Go to the fuse box/consumer unit and switch off the power. If you don't know which switch is the kitchen, flip the main switch to turn everything off. Only do this if you can reach it without walking through water.
3. Once the power is off, the dishwasher will stop and the extension lead will be safe. Then you can unplug things and mop up.

If you can't reach the fuse box safely, get everyone (and pets) out of the kitchen and call an electrician or your energy supplier's emergency line (in the UK, that's 105 for power emergencies).

Don't try to grab the extension lead or move it out of the way while the power is on.

## Once it's safe

The suds plus a leak at the front bottom of the door almost certainly mean the wrong detergent (like washing-up liquid) or far too much detergent. This is usually easy to fix:

• Scoop out the suds, then pour in a little vegetable oil or a splash of fabric softener, which helps break down foam.
• Run a short rinse cycle with no detergent, repeating until the suds are gone.
• In the future, use only proper dishwasher tablets/powder.

Before turning the power back on, make sure the floor, the extension lead, and the sockets are completely dry. If the extension lead got wet, throw it away rather than reusing it. If anything trips, sparks, or smells of burning, leave the power off and get an electrician.

You're doing the right thing by being careful. Turn the power off first, then deal with the rest.
ok im going to the fuse box now. the housemate used fairy washing up liquid cos we ran out of tablets, is that what caused it? the rcd hasnt tripped

## Yes, that's exactly what caused it

Washing-up liquid like Fairy is made to foam, and a dishwasher's spray turns even a small squirt into a huge amount of suds. They push out under the door seal. It's a very common mistake and usually does no lasting damage.

## Still switch it off, even though the RCD hasn't tripped

An RCD that hasn't tripped doesn't mean the area is safe. It only trips once current is already leaking, and water could still reach the extension lead at any moment. Switching off yourself is the right move.

• Switch off the main switch if you're not sure which circuit is the kitchen.
• Make sure your hands are dry and you're not standing in water.
• If the RCD trips by itself while you're there, or anything sparks or smells of burning, leave it all off.

## Once the power is off

1. Unplug the dishwasher and move the extension lead away from the water.
2. Mop up the floor with towels.
3. Scoop out as many suds from inside the dishwasher as you can with a cup or jug.
4. Let everything dry fully before turning the power back on. If the extension lead got wet, bin it.
5. Then run rinse cycles with no detergent until the suds are gone. A splash of fabric softener in the bottom can help kill the foam. It may take a couple of runs.

Until you get proper tablets, don't use any washing-up liquid in it, not even a drop. Hand wash for now instead.

Well done, the dangerous part is over.

## Clear the suds

1. Unplug the dishwasher and move the extension lead away from any wet areas.
2. Take out the dishes and rinse them in the sink.
3. Scoop out the suds and water from the bottom of the dishwasher with a cup or jug, then soak up the rest with a towel or sponge.
4. Kill the remaining foam. Sprinkle a handful of salt over it, or add a tablespoon of vegetable oil or a splash of fabric softener. Any of these will collapse the bubbles.
5. Take out and rinse the filter at the bottom of the tub. It usually twists out. Rinse it under the tap to get the soapy residue off.
6. Mop the floor and wipe under the door edge, where suds tend to hide.

## Getting the power back on

• Wait until the floor, sockets, and extension lead are completely dry. If the extension lead got wet, bin it rather than reusing it.
• If you used the main switch, your fridge and freezer are off. Once the kitchen is dry, you can turn the power back on. Keep the dishwasher unplugged until you're ready to run it.
• If the RCD trips, or anything sparks or smells of burning, switch off again and call an electrician.

## Rinse it out

Run a short or rinse cycle with no detergent and stay nearby. If suds appear at the door, stop it, scoop them out, and repeat. It often takes 2 or 3 runs to clear all the residue.

## About the landlord

This is a really common mistake and almost never damages the machine. Once the suds are gone, it should work normally. You may not need to tell them anything, but do let them know if:

• it keeps leaking after the suds are completely gone,
• it shows an error code or won't run, or
• water got under the kitchen units or flooring (look for swelling, damp, or a musty smell over the next few days).

Being upfront early is much better than a problem getting worse unnoticed. Most landlords would rather hear "we used the wrong soap, it leaked, we cleaned up" than discover damp later.
